introScreens.headline: What Happened on Mars in 2018
introScreens.bodyText: In 2018, NASA saw a small dust storm on Mars. It grew around the planet, more than 37 miles high! So noon turned pitch black. Solar-powered Opportunity lost power. Curiosity kept working on nuclear power.
introScreens.nasaSource: NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter & Mars Exploration Rover Mission Archives (2018)
introScreens.guideLine: Hi, I'm Pip! Captain Nova is our commander. She'll give you hints. Let's go!

introScreens.headline: NASA's Next Big Step: Moon to Mars
introScreens.bodyText: Astronauts on Mars will need power all Martian Sol. It runs oxygen makers, heat, and cold rocket fuel. Big storms return, so NASA is building nuclear fission power. Bases won't need sunlight alone.
introScreens.nasaSource: NASA Moon to Mars Architecture & Fission Surface Power Studies
introScreens.guideLine: Did you know? Real bases will need power day and night. That's your job soon!

introScreens.headline: May 2038: What Would You Do?
introScreens.bodyText: It is May 2038 at Ares Base. A giant Planet-Encircling Dust Event hits. Mars has very thin air and a 22-minute radio delay. Turning gear off saves energy. Only sunlight or nuclear power makes more!
introScreens.nasaSource: Future 2038 Scenario Built From Real Mars Year 34 (2018) Storm Data
introScreens.guideLine: Whoa, a giant storm is coming! Your crew needs you. Ready to lead?

kidGlossary.headline: Spotted From Mars Orbit in 2018
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On May 30, 2018, a NASA orbiter photographed a small dust cloud. Within days it grew into a storm around the whole planet. Weather cameras in space give early warning.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A dust storm starts when the Sun heats thin air. The air lifts red dust into spinning clouds. Clouds can grow and join.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter captured this daily global map showing a fast-growing Martian dust storm cloud spreading across Perseverance Valley.

kidGlossary.headline: The Storm Rose 37 Miles High
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Winds lifted red dust more than 37 miles into the sky. That is seven times higher than airplanes fly on Earth. The dust even hid Mars's giant volcanoes from space cameras.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: 37 miles is about seven times higher than airplanes fly. The dust went far above normal clouds.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: An orbital view over Mars reveals how towering dust plumes rose more than 37 miles into the sky and blurred giant volcanoes beneath.

kidGlossary.headline: Why Opportunity Went Quiet
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Opportunity explored Mars for over 14 years using solar panels. In 2018, dust blocked 97% of sunlight. Its batteries ran out in the cold dark. NASA called for it many times, but it never answered.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Opportunity was a golf-cart-sized rover. Two flat solar wings soaked up sunlight. That charged its batteries.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A NASA photograph of the Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity with its twin solar array wings spread wide to gather Martian sunlight.

kidGlossary.headline: Curiosity Kept Working
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Curiosity is far across Mars in Gale Crater. It kept doing science during the 2018 storm. It has a sealed nuclear battery. The battery turns heat into electricity without sunlight.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Curiosity did not shut down in the storm. It makes electricity from heat. The heat comes from a sealed nuclear battery.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA technicians at Kennedy Space Center install Curiosity's Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG) nuclear power unit before launch.

kidGlossary.headline: A Sol Is a Mars Day
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: One day on Mars is called a Sol. It lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes. That is a bit longer than an Earth day. Mars crews follow Mars time.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A Sol is one full day and night on Mars. It is 39 minutes longer than an Earth day.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's InSight lander instruments sit on rusty Martian soil where every sunrise and sunset marks another 24-hour-39-minute Martian Sol.

kidGlossary.headline: Mars Air Is Super Thin
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Mars's air is 100 times thinner than Earth's! A 60 mph Martian wind feels like a gentle breeze. It will not knock down a base. But tiny dust still covers panels.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Mars has very little air. It is about 1% as thick as Earth's air. Even fast winds push only softly.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A thin blue-tinted slice of Mars's wispy atmosphere photographed from orbit—too thin to knock down habitats, yet able to carry powdery dust.

kidGlossary.headline: Sticky Red Dust
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Martian dust is finer than baby powder. It has static charge. It clings to solar panels like dust on a rubbed balloon. It also sneaks into wheel joints.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Martian soil is crushed into fine powder. It holds static electricity. The grains cling to glass, seals, and solar wings.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Close-up microscopic view of fine red Martian grit photographed by NASA's Opportunity rover while exploring Meridiani Planum.

kidGlossary.headline: Noon Turned Pitch Black
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 10, 2018, dust above Opportunity got super thick. It blocked 97% of sunlight. High noon looked darker than a moonless night on Earth.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Dust in the air can get very thick. Then 97% of light is blocked. Even at noon, it looks like midnight.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A NASA sunlight simulation showing how clear noon on Mars on the left plunged into pitch darkness on June 10, 2018 on the right.

kidGlossary.headline: Rocket Fuel Needs Cool Power
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Future Mars rockets use liquid oxygen and methane fuel. It must stay super cold at -297°F. Electric chillers keep it cold. Without power, the fuel warms up and boils off.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Return rockets use fuel chilled below -297°F. If the coolers stop, the icy liquid warms up. Then it boils away as gas.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA orbital cooling hardware designed to test how super-cold liquid rocket propellant can be stored without warming and boiling away.

kidGlossary.headline: Dust Makes a Heat Blanket
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: In 2018, NASA found a strange twist. Thick dust made Mars days cooler by blocking sunlight. But nights got warmer! The dust trapped heat like a giant red blanket.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Floating dust acts like a blanket over Mars. By day it blocks sunlight. By night it keeps ground heat from escaping.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Curiosity rover photos from the June 2018 global storm showing dimmed afternoon light while thick dust trapped heat near the ground at night.

kidGlossary.headline: Radio Messages Take Time
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Radio signals between Mars and Earth take 6 to 22 minutes one way. Asking a question and hearing back can take up to 44 minutes. Mars crews must think for themselves!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Mars and Earth are millions of miles apart. Radio messages take up to 22 minutes one way. You can't chat with Mission Control live.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: One of NASA's giant 70-meter Deep Space Network dish antennas that beams and receives radio signals between Earth and Mars.

kidGlossary.headline: A Storm Around the Whole Planet
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 20, 2018, NASA called the storm a Planet-Encircling Dust Event. One big orange dust cloud wrapped all the way around Mars.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: This storm gets huge. Dust wraps around every side of Mars.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Two NASA global views of Mars taken weeks apart in 2018: clear craters before the storm on the left, and a planet-wide dust blanket on the right.

kidGlossary.headline: Dust Devils Clean Panels
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Years ago, Spirit and Opportunity sometimes got cleaned by dust devils. These tiny whirlwinds swept their panels clear. But no lucky gust helped Opportunity in 2018.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A dust devil is a small spinning whirlwind. It can brush a rover. It sweeps sticky red dust off solar panels.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A sunlit NASA rover photo showing a whirling Martian dust devil sweeping across crater plains like a natural broom.

kidGlossary.headline: Curiosity's Dusty Storm Selfie
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 15, 2018, Curiosity took a selfie in Gale Crater. Thick orange haze hid the far crater rim. Its nuclear power kept its science tools running.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Curiosity held out its camera arm for a selfie in Gale Crater. Brown haze hid the faraway mountain rim.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's Curiosity rover photographed itself on June 15, 2018, surrounded by thick brown dust haze while its nuclear battery kept tools running.

kidGlossary.headline: Nuclear Power for Dark Days
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA is testing small Fission Surface Power reactors. They make steady electricity day and night. That could protect future explorers during weeks of dusty darkness.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Nuclear fission splits atoms inside a sealed core. That makes steady electricity and heat. It works day and night, even in dusty darkness.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Concept artwork from NASA Glenn Research Center showing a Fission Surface Power reactor delivering nonstop electricity without sunlight.

kidGlossary.headline: Making Oxygen From Mars Air
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Mars's air is 95% carbon dioxide. A toaster-sized machine called MOXIE flew on Perseverance. It split Martian air into pure oxygen to breathe. It works a bit like a tree!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Oxygen generators take carbon dioxide from Mars's air. They split off pure oxygen. Astronauts get clean air to breathe.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's gold-coated MOXIE experiment aboard Perseverance—a real machine tested on Mars to turn carbon dioxide air into breathable oxygen.

kidGlossary.headline: Storms Lift Water Into the Sky
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA found that giant dust storms warm Mars's thin air. The warm air lifts hidden water vapor about 50 miles up. There, sunlight breaks the water apart. Crews must protect their water!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Water vapor is invisible water gas in the air. Dust storms warm the sky. They carry water far up, where sunlight splits it.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A NASA atmospheric map showing how Martian dust storms lift warm water vapor high above the surface into sunlight-exposed skies.

kidGlossary.headline: Greenhouses Grow Fresh Food
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA designers plan indoor Mars greenhouses with grow lights. Crews could grow fresh food when storms block the Sun. Tasty veggies also lift spirits!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Hydroponic plants grow in mineral water instead of soil. Pink and purple LED lights stand in for sunlight.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA greenhouse researchers testing leafy food crops under specialized indoor grow lights built for future off-world habitats.

kidGlossary.headline: Zapping Dust Off Suits
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Engineers tested wire grids that zap static dust off spacesuits and glass. That keeps sharp Martian dust out of astronaut lungs.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: An electrostatic dust shield has thin wires in glass or suit fabric. Tiny electric waves push static-clingy dust right off.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Engineers at NASA Kennedy Space Center testing an Electrodynamic Dust Shield that pulses electric fields to shake sticky dust off surfaces.

kidGlossary.headline: A Sky Tower Above Mars
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is like a tower in the sky. It takes wide storm photos. It also passes radio signals to Earth, even through dust.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: An orbital relay is a satellite high above Mars. It spots storms from space. It passes radio messages between astronauts and Earth.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Artist illustration of NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter circling Mars to capture storm maps and relay radio data back to Earth.

storyNodes.title: Sol 1: Dust Storm Alarm
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Satellites in space spotted a small storm before it grew huge.
storyNodes.storyText: Look out! Orbiting satellites just spotted a tiny dust storm heading your way. The sky is bright this Martian Sol as dust lifts water vapor.

choiceA.description: Bring astronauts inside and pack solar power into batteries.
choiceA.outcomeText: Batteries fill with power! The crew is safe inside, but stops outdoor work.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity ran on solar power for 14 years. A giant storm blocked the sun.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Without power, robots and heaters freeze in the deep Martian cold.
choiceA.imageCaption: This artist's illustration shows NASA's InSight lander on the surface of Mars, with its solar arrays deployed.
choiceA.guideReaction: Full batteries! Smart move before the sky goes dark.

choiceB.description: Let the crew collect ice and fill oxygen tanks.
choiceB.outcomeText: Oxygen tanks are full! The drill motors use lots of battery power.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Curiosity used a tiny nuclear battery. It kept rolling right through the storm.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Nuclear power does not need sunlight to make electricity.
choiceB.imageCaption: An electrical cable can be seen snaking its way along insulation material in this image of the interior of the Mars 2020 spacecraft at it cruises through interplanetary space to the Red Planet.
choiceB.guideReaction: Lots of oxygen! Pumps use power, but fresh air is great.

choiceC.description: Bring the crew inside and turn on electric dust shields.
choiceC.outcomeText: Electric shields push dust away from solar panels and airlocks!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: NASA created shields that use static electricity to push away dust.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars dust carries static cling, just like dust on a TV screen.
choiceC.imageCaption: Partially obscured by the Canadarm2, or Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS), arm the Space Shuttle Atlantis (background) moves toward the International Space Station (ISS) during rendezvous operations.
choiceC.guideReaction: Zap! The electric shields shake the red dust away!

storyNodes.guideTip: Whoa! A Sol is one day on Mars. It is slightly longer than Earth days!
storyNodes.novaHint: The storm is coming. Think about saving power before dust blocks sunlight.

storyNodes.title: Sol 2: Dust Hits Panels
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: In 2018, rising dust forced Opportunity to stop driving.

consequences.text: Sol 1 extra battery charge helped (+3% Electricity), but missing ice frustrated crew (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: A giant dust wall towers more than 37 miles high! Sticky red grit clings to panels. You must also keep rocket fuel cold.

choiceA.description: Chill rocket fuel and dim hallway lights to save power.
choiceA.outcomeText: Rocket fuel stays freezing cold! Hallways are dim, but batteries stay safe.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Rocket fuel must stay colder than winter ice so it does not boil.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Liquid fuel boils away into gas if tanks get too warm.
choiceA.imageCaption: This illustration shows a concept of how the NASA Mars Ascent Vehicle, carrying tubes containing rock and soil samples, could be launched from the surface of Mars in one step of the Mars sample return mission.
choiceA.guideReaction: Brrr! Hallways are chilly, but the escape rocket is safe!

choiceB.description: Use battery power to make fresh, clean oxygen.
choiceB.outcomeText: Crisp oxygen fills every room! The crew feels great, but batteries drain.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: NASA tested MOXIE on Mars. It pulls breathable oxygen right from thin air.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide, which humans cannot breathe.
choiceB.imageCaption: MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) was launched aboard NASA's Perseverance rover to test a technology for extracting oxygen from the Red Planet's carbon dioxide-rich atmosphere.
choiceB.guideReaction: Deep breath! Clean oxygen makes everyone smile and work happily.

choiceC.description: Power up the dish to track the storm from orbit.
choiceC.outcomeText: Clear radar maps show the storm! Running the dish heater uses power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Orbiting satellites tracked the 2018 dust storm every single day.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Satellites fly high above storms to guide rovers safely.
choiceC.imageCaption: Workers at NASA Deep Space Network Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex prepare a support leg that would help raise a portion of the giant Mars antenna.
choiceC.guideReaction: We see the whole storm! Look at that giant swirling cloud!

storyNodes.guideTip: The storm is huge! It is taller than seven Mount Everests stacked up!
storyNodes.novaHint: Cold fuel is heavy. Balance rocket coolers with life support power.

storyNodes.title: Sol 2: Yellow Grid Warning
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Mars dust clings to solar panels like static on clothes.

consequences.text: Full oxygen tanks from Sol 1 kept crew energized (+5% Crew Health), using power (-4% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust covers your panels, just like on Opportunity rover! Oxygen is high, but greenhouse crops need light. Red sticky grit is everywhere.

choiceA.description: Turn off plant grow-lights to save electricity for basic needs.
choiceA.outcomeText: Saving power keeps the base alive! The plants grow slower in the dark.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts will grow fresh greens in space to stay strong and healthy.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Plants turn light and water into fresh food and clean oxygen.
choiceA.imageCaption: Water and nutrients are being added to plants in the Veggie hardware in NASA Kennedy Space Center's ISS environment simulator chamber.
choiceA.guideReaction: Lights off saves power! The lettuce will take a little nap.

choiceB.description: Spend battery power on bright grow-lights for fresh veggies.
choiceB.outcomeText: Fresh salad lifts everyone's spirits! Battery power drops down lower.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts on the space station grow fresh salads under bright LED lights.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Fresh vitamins keep human minds sharp during long space voyages.
choiceB.imageCaption: This nickel-alloy heat exchanger is among several that were 3D printed for the Mars Oxygen In-situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE), one of the instruments aboard NASA's Perseverance Mars rover.
choiceB.guideReaction: Mmm, fresh green snacks! The crew is super happy today.

choiceC.description: Turn up the backup nuclear reactor to make steady electricity.
choiceC.outcomeText: The reactor hums with power! It generates electricity without any sun.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: NASA tested small nuclear reactors to power future human Mars bases.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Nuclear reactors make electricity through day, night, and giant storms.
choiceC.imageCaption: NASA's Curiosity Mars rover demonstrated a new multitasking capability when capturing this view: It snapped the 15 images that make up the mosaic while simultaneously communicating with an orbiter.
choiceC.guideReaction: Power surge! The tiny nuclear core makes steady watts in the dark.

storyNodes.guideTip: Plants in the greenhouse need bright lamps because Mars is dim!
storyNodes.novaHint: Plants make food, but need power. Decide how much energy to spend.

storyNodes.title: Sol 2: Dust on Airlocks
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Static electric charge makes Mars dust cling to everything.

consequences.text: Clean Sol 1 dust shields saved gear (+4% Crew Health), using power (-4% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: Electric shields fight off sticky red grit. We cannot wait for dust devils! Fine powder drifts toward airlock suit doors.

choiceA.description: Power door cleaners so zero dust enters astronaut lungs.
choiceA.outcomeText: Airlocks stay clean and dust-free! The door shields use steady power.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: NASA designs suits that stay outside the cabin to block poisonous dust.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Breathing sharp mineral dust can hurt astronaut lungs.
choiceA.imageCaption: Astronaut Peggy A.
choiceA.guideReaction: Puff! High-voltage zap cleans suits before astronauts step inside.

choiceB.description: Connect nuclear power straight to batteries and dim heaters.
choiceB.outcomeText: Batteries charge steadily! Corridors are chilly, but power is strong.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Engineers route nuclear electricity to protect life-support batteries first.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Nuclear power provides constant electricity without cloudy day drops.
choiceB.imageCaption: In the high bay of the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility (PHSF) at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, spacecraft technicians from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory guide a turning fixture onto the multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) for NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission.
choiceB.guideReaction: Nice connection! Power flows right where we need it most.

choiceC.description: Send crew outside to add weatherproof shields to electronics.
choiceC.outcomeText: Electronics are safe from grit! The outdoor walk tired the crew.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Spacewalks on Mars take careful effort because spacesuits are stiff.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Spacesuit gloves make simple tool work feel like squeezing tennis balls.
choiceC.imageCaption: Astronaut Peggy A.
choiceC.guideReaction: Good job fixing the box! Those spacesuits are heavy work.

storyNodes.guideTip: Mars dust is like tiny bits of broken glass. Keep it outside!
storyNodes.novaHint: Clean airlocks protect human lungs. Balance door shields with power.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Red Dusk Falling
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Dust traps daytime heat, making cold Mars nights warmer.

consequences.text: Locked chillers saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but chilly halls gave stiff joints (-4% Crew Health).
Sleeping crops saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but missing fresh veggies lowers stamina (-5% Crew Health).
Sol 1 extra battery charge still cushions the power grid (+3% Electricity).
Reserve oxygen from Sol 1 keeps air fresh (+4% Crew Health), using valve power (-3% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust dims the Sun in thin Martian air! Dust starts a heat blanket at dusk as oxygen generators pull power.

choiceA.description: Close empty side labs and gather the crew in central bunks.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sealing side labs saves big power! Outer halls get icy cold.
choiceA.bonusNote: Because you overcharged batteries on Sol 1, locking down side labs seals in an extra +3% Electricity saved reserve!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts close doors between modules to trap warm air and save power.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Closing hatches prevents cold drafts from spreading across the station.
choiceA.imageCaption: The EMIT instrument after completion of all pre-launch environmental testing.
choiceA.guideReaction: Hatches sealed tight! Heat stays inside the center habitat.

choiceB.description: Spend battery power to scrub carbon dioxide and pump oxygen.
choiceB.outcomeText: Crisp oxygen fills living rooms! The heavy air pumps use power.
choiceB.bonusNote: Your Sol 1 spare oxygen stockpile cuts compressor workload, saving +3% Electricity saved during the purge!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Life support systems must scrub carbon dioxide so humans can breathe clean air.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Without scrubbers, carbon dioxide builds up and makes astronauts sleepy.
choiceB.imageCaption: Engineers lower MOXIE (the Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment) into the belly of NASA's Perseverance rover.
choiceB.guideReaction: Ahhh, fresh air! Crisp oxygen helps everyone think clearly.

choiceC.description: Download satellite storm maps so astronauts stay safe indoors.
choiceC.outcomeText: Satellites show storm tracks! Downloading radar maps uses modest power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Satellites in high orbit track dust fronts and beam weather maps down.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Orbiters can see storm fronts hundreds of miles away.
choiceC.imageCaption: As part of a major refurbishment for the giant Mars antenna at NASA Deep Space Network Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex, a stringer box is lowered into place.
choiceC.guideReaction: Radar locked! Now we know exactly when gusts hit.

storyNodes.guideTip: Even in thin air, dust traps warm heat near the ground at night!
storyNodes.novaHint: When solar fades, manage your life support and heater watts carefully.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Sky Dimming Fast
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Mars dust storms can swallow the entire planet in days.

consequences.text: Boosted MOXIE oxygen keeps crew sharp (+5% Crew Health), using power (-4% Power).
Fresh salad greens boost crew stamina (+5% Crew Health), using power (-4% Power).
Electric airlock shields keep dust out of lungs (+4% Crew Health), using power (-3% Power).
Sol 1 dust shields shook static grit off panels (0% Electricity Conserved!).

storyNodes.storyText: Dusk falls at noon as a planet-wide storm grows! The sky nears noon pitch black. Greenhouse crops compete with sensors for power.

choiceA.description: Dim cabin lights and heaters to save power before blackout.
choiceA.outcomeText: Saving power protects the batteries! Rooms are chilly and dim.
choiceA.bonusNote: Your Sol 2 electrostatic airlock seals keep dust out during power cutbacks, softening Crew Health loss by +5%!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Spacecraft turn off non-essential instruments during power emergencies.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Cutting cabin lights saves precious battery watts for life support.
choiceA.imageCaption: Outredgeous red leaf lettuce, Mizuna mustard and Waldmann's green lettuce are growing in the Veggie control system in the ISS environment simulator chamber in the Space Station Processing Facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
choiceA.guideReaction: Heaters dimmed! Every saved watt keeps life support alive.

choiceB.description: Keep bright lights glowing so fresh crops keep growing.
choiceB.outcomeText: Fresh green sprouts lift spirits! The grow-lights draw heavy power.
choiceB.bonusNote: Because you kept the greenhouse lit on Sol 2, plants skipped an expensive cold-start—saving +3% Electricity saved!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts grow fresh salad crops under LED lamps for vitamins.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Plants provide psychological comfort along with fresh oxygen and nutrition.
choiceB.imageCaption: ray image shows the interior of a palm-size 3D-printed heat exchanger inside Perseverance's Mars Oxygen In-situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE) instrument.
choiceB.guideReaction: Yum, crunchy fresh leaves! The crew is smiling big.

choiceC.description: Cut crew heaters to power wind radar and study the storm.
choiceC.outcomeText: Sensors track the storm front! Chilly drafts sweep the dorms.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Scientists track atmospheric pressure to understand how dust storms grow.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Understanding storm physics helps NASA design safer future habitats.
choiceC.imageCaption: The giant Mars antenna at NASA Deep Space Network Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex replaced four elevation bearings as part of a major refurbishment.
choiceC.guideReaction: Science data incoming! Fascinating storm measurements today.

storyNodes.guideTip: The storm wraps around the whole planet! There is no escape route.
storyNodes.novaHint: A whole-planet storm lasts weeks. Pace food, water, and power.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Nuclear Core Hums
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Nuclear generators keep running right through deep darkness.

consequences.text: Nuclear power gave steady electricity (+3% Electricity), but loud shielding bunks tired crew (-4% Crew Health).
Direct reactor connection filled batteries (+3% Electricity), but cold galley lowered comfort (-4% Crew Health).
Oxygen stockpile keeps air easy to breathe (+4% Crew Health), using minor power (-3% Power).
Sol 1 dust shields shook static grit off panels (0% Electricity Conserved!).

storyNodes.storyText: Red dusk falls, but just like Curiosity kept working, your nuclear power plant hums! You must also keep rocket fuel cold.

choiceA.description: Move astronauts into narrow ground tunnels to save fan power.
choiceA.outcomeText: Tunnels save heating power! Tight bunks make sleep uncomfortable.
choiceA.bonusNote: Extra Sol 1 oxygen bottles freshen the cramped tunnel air, saving +4% Crew Health!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars dirt protects astronauts from space radiation and temperature swings.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Burying habitats under regolith dirt provides natural thermal insulation.
choiceA.imageCaption: Astronauts Piers J. Sellers (left ) and David A. Wolf work on the newly installed Starboard One (S1) truss to the International Space Station (ISS) during the STS-112 mission.
choiceA.guideReaction: Cozy underground! Natural dirt keeps the cold wind away.

choiceB.description: Run cooling fans at full speed so crew stays comfortable.
choiceB.outcomeText: The reactor core stays cool and happy! Batteries drop down.
choiceB.bonusNote: Pre-warmed fission coolant loops from Sol 2 stabilize faster, saving +4% cooling Power!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Nuclear systems need radiator fans to dump extra heat safely.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Radiators pump fluid through fins to radiate heat into space.
choiceB.imageCaption: In the high bay of the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility (PHSF) at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, spacecraft technicians from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory position the multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) for NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission on the turning fixture above the MMRTG integration cart.
choiceB.guideReaction: Cool and steady! The reactor hums smoothly tonight.

choiceC.description: Send crew outside to bolt protective dust covers onto turbines.
choiceC.outcomeText: Turbines are shielded from grit! The dusty outdoor walk tired crew.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Covering mechanical joints keeps fine grit from grinding gears down.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Sharp Martian dust acts like sandpaper on moving turbine parts.
choiceC.imageCaption: In the high bay of the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility (PHSF) at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, spacecraft technicians from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory guide the multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) for NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission on the turning fixture toward the MMRTG integration cart.
choiceC.guideReaction: Turbine covers bolted! The cooling fins are safe from grit.

storyNodes.guideTip: The nuclear reactor makes electricity inside, even when the sun vanishes!
storyNodes.novaHint: Nuclear power is steady. Decide whether to cool equipment or crew.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Radio Static Haze
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Satellites fly high above storms to relay radio signals.

consequences.text: Satellite weather maps boosted crew readiness (+4% Crew Health), using power (-3% Power).
Cleaned panels kept power flow steady (0% Electricity Conserved!), but dust irritated throats (-4% Crew Health).
Sol 1 battery vault still cushions the darkening sky (+3% Electricity).
Sol 1 dust shields continue repelling fine grit outdoors (0% Electricity Conserved!).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust haze creates a murky sky view! An orbital satellite talks across a 22-minute radio delay as electric shields hum.

choiceA.description: Turn off radio dish heaters to save battery power before blackout.
choiceA.outcomeText: Saving power protects the batteries! We lose live messages from Earth.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Turning off powerful transmitters saves big wattage during storms.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: High-gain antennas use lots of electricity to beam signals to Earth.
choiceA.imageCaption: The solar arrays on NASA's InSight Mars lander were deployed as part of testing conducted Jan. 23, 2018, at Lockheed Martin Space in Littleton, Colorado.
choiceA.guideReaction: Antennas sleeping! That saves lots of power for life support.

choiceB.description: Send crew outside to crimp tight dust sleeves over junction boxes.
choiceB.outcomeText: Junction boxes are sealed from grit! Cold windy work tired the crew.
choiceB.bonusNote: Extra Sol 1 battery voltage powers electric crimping tools faster, locking in +3% Electricity saved!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts wrap wiring boxes with silicone sleeves to stop shorts.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Dry static dust can cause electrical sparks if it gets inside plugs.
choiceB.imageCaption: A view of Extravehicular Mobility Units (EMUs) in the Quest Airlock (A/L) aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
choiceB.guideReaction: Cables sealed tight! No short circuits will happen here.

choiceC.description: Plug pressurized rover fuel cells into the habitat filter bus.
choiceC.outcomeText: Rover fuel cells share extra power! Cabin air stays warm and clean.
choiceC.bonusNote: Because your Sol 1 EDS power junction already uses standard ISS-Mars dome plugs, linking the rover bus saves +3% Electricity saved!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Electric vehicles can feed battery power back into buildings in emergencies.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Connecting rover batteries gives the habitat extra backup power.
choiceC.imageCaption: As part of a Mars sample return mission, a rocket will carry a container of sample tubes with Martian rock and soil samples into orbit around Mars and release it for pick up by another spacecraft.
choiceC.guideReaction: Rover connected! Extra power is flowing right into the habitat.

storyNodes.guideTip: Satellites in space act like cell towers to send radio messages home!
storyNodes.novaHint: Earth messages take 22 minutes. Rely on local plans and rovers.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Midnight at Noon
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: By Sol 4, the 2018 storm blocked 99% of daylight.

consequences.text: Sealed corridors save power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but chilly rooms stiffen joints (-4% Crew Health).
Pre-locked chillers saved battery voltage (0% Electricity Conserved!), but rationing lowered comfort (-3% Crew Health).
Sol 1 dust shields stopped electrical short circuits (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Rationed heat saved battery charge (0% Electricity Conserved!), but cold leaves crew stiff (-3% Crew Health).
Powering down the dish conserved electricity (0% Electricity Conserved!), but silence causes loneliness (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust blocks 97% of normal sunlight, just like on Opportunity rover! Batteries must fight to keep rocket fuel cold.

choiceA.description: Pump power into rocket chillers while crew bundles in coats.
choiceA.outcomeText: Rocket fuel stays safe and frozen! The habitat feels chilly.
choiceA.bonusNote: Because you locked the fuel chillers back on Sol 2, propellant pipes stayed extra cold and needed less electricity today (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Rocket propellants like liquid methane must stay chilled at -297°F.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: If tanks warm up, liquid fuel boils into gas and escapes into space.
choiceA.imageCaption: Angie Jackman, manager of the Mars Ascent Vehicle (MAV) project, holds a 3D-printed model of the tubes NASA's Perseverance rover is already filling with Martian rock and soil samples.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rocket fuel safe! Our ride back to Earth is protected.

choiceB.description: Dial back outdoor fuel chillers so the crew stays warm indoors.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm air fills the dome! Rocket tank gauges show slight warming.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Keeping astronauts warm prevents hypothermia and maintains mental focus.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Cold stress lowers human immune defenses and slows reaction times.
choiceB.imageCaption: and-rocket combination that would play a key role in returning to Earth samples of Mars material collected by the Perseverance rover.
choiceB.guideReaction: Nice and warm! Happy astronauts can solve any problem.

choiceC.description: Shut down science rooms and hallway heat to guard battery power.
choiceC.outcomeText: Battery drain stops! Astronauts rest quietly in dim, chilly bunks.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Deep space probes enter beacon mode to survive power emergencies.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Beacon mode runs only vital computer clocks and emergency radios.
choiceC.imageCaption: up image taken on Nov. 16, 2019, in High Bay 1 of the Spacecraft Assembly Facility at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
choiceC.guideReaction: Beacon mode locked! Every single watt is guarded.

storyNodes.guideTip: It is totally black at lunchtime! Solar panels make zero electricity.
storyNodes.novaHint: Solar is out. Protect the cold rocket fuel for your flight home.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Storm Peaks Outside
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Dust trapped near the ground acts like an insulating thermal blanket.

consequences.text: Greenhouse plant lights draw steady power (-4% Power), but fresh greens boost stamina (+5% Crew Health).
Clean MOXIE air purge from Sol 3 kept cabin air crisp and sharp (+5% Crew Health).
Upgraded suit seals stop fine red powder at the airlock (+4% Crew Health).
Tunnel bunks saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but tight quarters left muscles cramped (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust blocks 97% of normal sunlight! Thick dust acts like a blanket trapping heat near ground against airlock suitports.

choiceA.description: Turn down electric heaters and have everyone wear thick parkas.
choiceA.outcomeText: Thick parkas save power! Working in bulky coats tires the crew.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Thermal survival gear keeps astronauts warm when electrical heat is cut.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Multi-layer insulation traps body heat with reflective silver film.
choiceA.imageCaption: 104 mission specialist, participates in space history as he joins fellow astronaut and mission specialist Michael L.
choiceA.guideReaction: Parkas zipped up! Warm coats save lots of battery power.

choiceB.description: Run kitchen stoves and bright lamps for a happy hot dinner.
choiceB.outcomeText: Hot stew lifts everyone's spirits! Kitchen stoves use battery power.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Sharing a hot meal boosts team morale during dark space emergencies.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Warm comfort food keeps astronaut spirits high during long crises.
choiceB.imageCaption: NASA interns Jessica Scotten, left, and Ayla Grandpre water plants in the Veggie hardware in NASA Kennedy Space Center's ISS environment simulator chamber.
choiceB.guideReaction: Dinner is served! Hot food makes this dark day bright.

choiceC.description: Pressurize airlock doors so swirling grit cannot enter rooms.
choiceC.outcomeText: Door curtains keep dust out! Running the pumps uses battery power.
choiceC.bonusNote: Your Sol 2 suit-seal upgrades snap shut seamlessly with the airlock gates, keeping extra grit off crew lungs (+5% Crew Health)!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Positive air pressure pushes dust outward when airlock doors open.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Air pressure differences keep fine minerals from floating into cabins.
choiceC.imageCaption: NASA astronaut and Expedition 72 Commander Suni Williams works in the Quest airlock readying a pair of spacesuits that she and NASA astronaut Nick Hague will wear durimg a spacewalk to remove radio communications hardware and search for microbes outside the International Space Station.
choiceC.guideReaction: Air curtains on! Not a single speck of dust gets inside.

storyNodes.guideTip: The storm is at peak strength! The dust blanket keeps nights warmer.
storyNodes.novaHint: This is the darkest day. Keep crew morale strong and grit outside.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Clogged Air Filters
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Curiosity rolled on nuclear power while dust coated Gale Crater.

consequences.text: Sol 3 storm sensors still drain circuits (-5% Power), though alerts helped (+2% Crew Health).
Steady reactor cooling kept electronics safe (+3% Crew Health).
Reactor bypass overheated coils (-5% Power) and was noisy (-3% Crew Health).
Sealed power ducts protected cables from dust (0% Electricity Conserved!).

storyNodes.storyText: Curiosity rolled safely on nuclear power, but humans breathe air! Sticky red grit just clogged filters. The MOXIE oxygen maker needs airflow.

choiceA.description: Wear masks and clean dust out of main cabin air filters.
choiceA.outcomeText: Clean air flows through the dome! Cleaning filters was tiring work.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Space crews clean life support filters regularly to maintain clean air.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: HEPA air filters catch microscopic dust particles before lungs inhale them.
choiceA.imageCaption: The port side of NASA's Perseverance Mars rover can be seen in this image taken on Nov.
choiceA.guideReaction: Scrub scrub scrub! Clean airflow is back in every room.

choiceB.description: Keep fans running to save power without stopping to clean.
choiceB.outcomeText: Saving power protects batteries! Hazy cabin air makes crew cough.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Dust in cabin air causes eye irritation and respiratory coughing.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars mineral dust contains toxic perchlorates that irritate human lungs.
choiceB.imageCaption: NASA astronaut and Expedition 74 flight engineer Jack Hathaway configures a spacesuit installing its components, checking a helmet, and cleaning suit seals inside the International Space Station's Quest airlock.
choiceB.guideReaction: Cough cough! Dusty air saves power, but tickles throats.

choiceC.description: Turn on smaller backup scrubbers and vent dust outside.
choiceC.outcomeText: Backup scrubbers clear the haze! The extra motors draw power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Manned space habitats carry dual backup systems for all vital equipment.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Redundant backup scrubbers kick in when primary units get clogged.
choiceC.imageCaption: Workers at NASA Deep Space Network Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex check on a set of jacks used to raise the upper part of the giant Mars antenna.
choiceC.guideReaction: Backup scrubbers online! Fresh air without the tiring scrubbing.

storyNodes.guideTip: Human astronauts breathe air. Robots only need electrical power!
storyNodes.novaHint: Clogged filters strain lungs. Clean them now or switch to spares.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Signals in Blackout
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Orbiting satellites stayed high above the dust to relay commands.

consequences.text: Aligning dishes on Sol 3 saved radio power (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Rover heaters ate power (-4% Power), but rovers stayed safe (+4% Crew Health).
Sol 2 satellite link gave clear updates (+2% Crew Health).
Reactor turbine shields protected power flow (0% Electricity Conserved!).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust clouds tower more than 37 miles high! An MRO relay satellite flies overhead. Balance parked rovers with your nuclear power plant.

choiceA.description: Put outside rovers and antennas to sleep to save power.
choiceA.outcomeText: All watts stay inside the habitat! We lose satellite weather maps.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Probes sleep during deep cold to save battery life for emergencies.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Hibernating gear draws only tiny trickles of standby electricity.
choiceA.imageCaption: This artist's concept shows what Deep Space Station-23, a new antenna dish at the Deep Space Network's complex in Goldstone, California, will look like when complete in several years.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rovers sleeping! Every watt is saved for life support.

choiceB.description: Send crew out to hook rover batteries into the habitat grid.
choiceB.outcomeText: Rover batteries boost base power! Hauling heavy cables tired the crew.
choiceB.bonusNote: Sol 1 EDS junction buses and Chariot Rover connectors are already staged at the main Suitport, feeding extra charge straight in (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Electric vehicles can send battery power back into buildings in emergencies.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Connecting rover batteries gives the habitat a giant power bank.
choiceB.imageCaption: NASA astronaut and Expedition 74 flight engineer Jessica Meir works inside the International Space Station's Quest airlock, installing leg and arm components on a spacesuit and swapping components from one suit to another.
choiceB.guideReaction: Plugged in! The rovers are powering the lights right now.

choiceC.description: Power the dish to get new storm maps and notes from Earth.
choiceC.outcomeText: Family letters bring big smiles! The big radio dish uses power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts receive daily voice notes and emails from family on Earth.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Hearing loved ones is the number one morale booster in space.
choiceC.imageCaption: Work began on March 11, 2010 to replace a set of elevation bearings on the giant Mars antenna at NASA Deep Space Network complex in Goldstone, Calif.
choiceC.guideReaction: Letters from Earth! Everyone is smiling and reading warm notes.

storyNodes.guideTip: Satellites fly high in space where there is no dust storm at all!
storyNodes.novaHint: Satellites have storm maps from above. Think about connecting.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Gloomy Midpoint
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: In 2018, Opportunity went silent while storm winds lifted moisture skyward.

consequences.text: Sol 4 chilled fuel draws steady power (-5% Power), but calms the crew (+4% Crew Health).
Wearing parkas saved heating power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but heavy coats tire crew (-4% Crew Health).
Cold corridors save heating power (0% Electricity Conserved!), while frosty bulkheads chill crew (-4% Crew Health).
Sleeping rovers saved energy (0% Electricity Conserved!), but losing mobile eyes adds stress (-2% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Zero solar power for days! Winds lift water vapor skyward. Route watts from your nuclear reactor to keep rocket fuel cold or heat rooms.

choiceA.description: Spend electricity to keep return rocket fuel safely frozen.
choiceA.outcomeText: Rocket fuel stays freezing cold! The crew quarters feel chilly.
choiceA.bonusNote: Because you already froze the rocket fuel on Sol 4, chilled pipes need much less pump energy today (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Return rockets store liquid methane at super cold temperatures.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Tanks need chillers so fuel does not warm up and turn into gas.
choiceA.imageCaption: This artist concept of a proposed Mars sample return mission portrays the launch of an ascent vehicle. The solar panels in the foreground are part of a rover.
choiceA.guideReaction: Fuel chilled! The ticket home is safe and ready.

choiceB.description: Route heat inward for warm showers and healthy muscle stretches.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm water and stretches bring smiles! Battery reserves dip lower.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts exercise two hours daily to keep bones and muscles strong.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Zero gravity and cold rooms make muscles feel stiff without exercise.
choiceB.imageCaption: This image of the International Space Station (ISS) was photographed by one of the crewmembers of the STS-112 mission following separation from the Space Shuttle Orbiter Atlantis as the orbiter pulled away from the ISS.
choiceB.guideReaction: Warm showers! Everyone is stretching and feeling energized.

choiceC.description: Cut heat to outer exercise rooms to save battery power.
choiceC.outcomeText: Batteries stay rock steady! Frost creeps closer along the outer halls.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Spacecraft shut down non-vital rooms to protect battery reserves.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Saving power keeps essential computer clocks and air pumps alive.
choiceC.imageCaption: This image of the International Space Station (ISS) was photographed by one of the crewmembers of the STS-112 mission following separation from the Space Shuttle Orbiter Atlantis as the orbiter pulled away from the ISS.
choiceC.guideReaction: Blankets on! Conserving power keeps life support running.

storyNodes.guideTip: The storm is at its halfway point! Hang in there, space explorers!
storyNodes.novaHint: Check your nuclear watts. Keep the rocket safe without freezing crew rooms.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Cabin Fever Days
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Mars dust storms trap ground heat for weeks during twilight.

consequences.text: Lowering chillers saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but fuel worries stress crew (-4% Crew Health).
Hot meals used power (-4% Power), but kept crew spirits high (+5% Crew Health).
Clean Sol 4 filters keep fresh air flowing quietly (+5% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust keeps trapping heat outside. Five long Martian Sols in dim light make astronauts miss greenhouse crops and sun.

choiceA.description: Shut off outer bedroom heaters and camp together in command.
choiceA.outcomeText: Turning off bedroom heaters saves power! Crowded rooms make sleep noisy.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Crews gather in small, well-insulated cabins to stay warm together.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Grouping humans together shares natural body warmth efficiently.
choiceA.imageCaption: This image shows the Integrated Truss Assembly S-1 (S-One), the Starboard Side Thermal Radiator Truss, for the International Space Station (ISS) undergoing final construction in the Space Station manufacturing facility at the Marshall Space Flight Center.
choiceA.guideReaction: Campfire style! Cozy together, even if snoring is loud.

choiceB.description: Spend battery power on bright daylight lamps in private bunks.
choiceB.outcomeText: Bright daylight bulbs chase away gloom! Battery meters slide down.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Daylight lamps help astronauts regulate circadian sleep cycles.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Bright full-spectrum light tells the brain when to stay alert.
choiceB.imageCaption: DSS43 is a 70-meter-wide (230-feet-wide) radio antenna at the Deep Space Network's Canberra facility in Australia.
choiceB.guideReaction: Bright lights! It feels like a sunny spring morning inside.

choiceC.description: Pack astronauts into tight shelter bunks next to the reactor core.
choiceC.outcomeText: Shelter bunks save strong wattage! Stiff bunks leave backs sore.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Space habitats include small shielded areas for storm emergencies.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Thick water walls around storm shelters block cosmic radiation.
choiceC.imageCaption: In the high bay of the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility (PHSF) at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, the multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) for NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission is attached to the MMRTG integration cart.
choiceC.guideReaction: Shelter bunks locked! Big power saved, but tight sleeping.

storyNodes.guideTip: Staying inside for days is tough. Space crews play games to stay cheerful!
storyNodes.novaHint: Astronaut mood matters. Light and good rest keep your team sharp.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Dust Haze Inside
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Curiosity snapped a selfie showing fine dust covering its deck.

consequences.text: Bypassing clogged filters left fine dust in ducts (-6% Crew Health).
Tethered rover batteries supply power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but tracked grit indoors (-3% Crew Health).
Pressurized airlocks block outdoor dust, protecting breathing (+4% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Just like when haze coated lenses on Curiosity, sticky red grit dims base lamps. No dust devils are clearing panels today.

choiceA.description: Turn on loud medical air scrubbers to strip dust from rooms.
choiceA.outcomeText: Turbines trap the red haze quickly! Scrubbers draw heavy power.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Space air filters run multi-stage fans to capture floating dust.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Electrostatic plates pull charged dust grains right out of air.
choiceA.imageCaption: One investigation on NASA's Mars 2020 rover will extract oxygen from the Martian atmosphere. It is called MOXIE, for Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment.
choiceA.guideReaction: Vroooom! The big vacuums swallowed all that red dust.

choiceB.description: Save electricity by having crew wear paper filter masks all Sol.
choiceB.outcomeText: Saving power protects the batteries! Itchy masks make crew cough.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts wear masks whenever cabin dust levels rise above normal.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: N95-grade filters stop 95% of airborne mineral particles.
choiceB.imageCaption: Members of NASA's Mars 2020 project install the Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE) into the chassis of NASA's next Mars rover.
choiceB.guideReaction: Masks on! Power is safe, but noses feel itchy.

choiceC.description: Drive outside rovers to pulse electric shields on outer vents.
choiceC.outcomeText: Rovers sweep outdoor vents clear! Clean air flows back inside.
choiceC.bonusNote: Because you insulated EDS controller boxes back on Sol 2, pressurized sensors shed dust twice as fast (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Remote rovers can clear vents without risking astronaut spacewalks.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Robotic arms perform delicate exterior brush work in toxic air.
choiceC.imageCaption: NASA astronaut and Expedition 74 flight engineer Jack Hathaway configures a spacesuit installing its components, checking a helmet, and cleaning suit seals inside the International Space Station's Quest airlock.
choiceC.guideReaction: Good little rovers! They cleaned vents without any spacewalk.

storyNodes.guideTip: Curiosity took a photo of itself covered in red dust. Say cheese!
storyNodes.novaHint: Fine dust irritates lungs. Clean the air before crew stamina drops.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Radio Wait in Blackout
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Earth radio signals take 22 minutes to travel to Mars.

consequences.text: Beacon mode saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but dark rooms stressed crew (-4% Crew Health).
Orbiter pings used power (-4% Power), but family mail boosted morale (+5% Crew Health).
Auxiliary scrubbers ran smoothly (0% Electricity Conserved!) and kept air fresh (+3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Satellites show this is a planet-wide storm! An MRO relay satellite passes overhead across the 22-minute radio delay.

choiceA.description: Power down deep-space dishes and rec rooms to save electricity.
choiceA.outcomeText: Batteries conserve every watt! Radio silence leaves crew lonely.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Cutting radio amplifiers saves dozens of kilowatts during emergencies.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Deep space transmitters need powerful water-cooled tubes to broadcast.
choiceA.imageCaption: The antenna of the Deep Space Network's Deep Space Station 43 (DSS-43) in Canberra, Australia, spans 70 meters (230 foot) and stands 73 meters (239 foot), dwarfing workers as they perform upgrades on the central cone that contains sensitive transmitters and receivers.
choiceA.guideReaction: Radios off! Power is guarded, but the room is quiet.

choiceB.description: Spend power warming sleeping bunks and cleaning cabin air.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm vents ease tired muscles! Battery reserves drop down lower.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Comfortable living temperatures help astronauts recover from stress.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Warm air and good sleep help human immune cells stay active.
choiceB.imageCaption: In the high bay of the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility (PHSF) at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, a crane lifts the multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) for NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission from its support base, at left, toward the MMRTG integration cart behind it.
choiceB.guideReaction: Warm and cozy! Rest is the best medicine for the crew.

choiceC.description: Use radio dish to send storm readings and download Earth mail.
choiceC.outcomeText: Fresh weather maps and Earth notes cheer everyone! Power drops.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars orbiters store and forward gigabytes of science data daily.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: High-speed lasers and radio dishes bridge the space gap home.
choiceC.imageCaption: In a delicate operation, a 400-ton crane lifts the new X-band cone into the 70-meter (230-foot) Deep Space Network's Deep Space Station 43 (DSS-43) dish in Canberra, Australia.
choiceC.guideReaction: Mail call! Cheerful voices from Earth make hearts light.

storyNodes.guideTip: By the time Earth answers, 44 minutes pass! You are in charge here.
storyNodes.novaHint: You make the calls. Decide whether to spend power on radio or warmth.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: Cut Off by Dust
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Storm winds in 100x thinner air carry dust, not physical force.

consequences.text: Fuel chillers draw power (-4% Power), but safe launch fuel calms crew (+3% Crew Health).
Overcharged cells from Sol 1 still supply backup voltage (+3% Electricity).
Locked chillers save grid power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but chill halls (-3% Crew Health).
Chiller pumps used battery power (-4% Power), but kept fuel tanks ice-cold (+4% Crew Health).
Camping in central hub saved heat (0% Electricity Conserved!), though noise ruined sleep (-4% Crew Health).
Cutting lounge power preserved reserves (0% Electricity Conserved!), but silence felt lonely (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Weeks ago satellites spotted a tiny dust storm. Now thin Martian air cuts you off across a 22-minute radio delay.

choiceA.description: Spend battery power to send storm readings and stream family voices.
choiceA.outcomeText: Family voices echo across space! Transmitting uses heavy power.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Giant antenna dishes on Earth listen for faint signals from Mars.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Signals take 22 minutes to travel across 150 million miles.
choiceA.imageCaption: Located in Canberra, Australia, the Deep Space Network's Deep Space Station 43 spans 70 meters (230 feet), making it the largest steerable parabolic antenna in the Southern Hemisphere.
choiceA.guideReaction: Hello Earth! Hearing family voices makes everyone smile warmly.

choiceB.description: Switch off big transmitters so all electricity stays in batteries.
choiceB.outcomeText: Power bars hold completely steady! Silent rooms deepen homesickness.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Spacecraft hold radio silence to conserve power during dark flybys.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio transmitters are among the heaviest electrical draws on board.
choiceB.imageCaption: While in the landed configuration for the last time before arriving on Mars, NASA's InSight lander was commanded to deploy its solar arrays to test and verify the exact process that it will use on the surface of the Red Planet.
choiceB.guideReaction: Quiet base! Batteries are safe and sound for tomorrow.

choiceC.description: Fly a tough little drone above dust to see if skies are clearing.
choiceC.outcomeText: The drone spots thinning dust above! Flying the drone uses power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: NASA flew the Ingenuity helicopter over 70 times in thin Mars air.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Drone blades must spin 2,400 times a minute in thin air.
choiceC.imageCaption: part of NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN) – carried out a test to receive data from the agency's Voyager 1 spacecraft at the same time on April 20, 2024.
choiceC.guideReaction: Look at the drone fly! It sees blue sky peeking through!

storyNodes.guideTip: Thin air means wind can lift tiny dust, but cannot blow you away!
storyNodes.novaHint: Six Sols in the dark is tough. Keep communication and drones ready.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: Fresh Veggie Dreams
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: One Mars Sol is about 24 hours and 39 minutes long.

consequences.text: Warmed gym gear from Sol 5 kept muscles limber and strong (+4% Crew Health).
Bright daylight lamps restored natural sleep cycles (+5% Crew Health), using power (-4% Power).
Heavy scrubbers cleared red haze (+4% Crew Health), but drew power (-5% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: Six long rounds of a Martian Sol make astronauts crave greenhouse crops! Run the MOXIE oxygen maker or save electricity.

choiceA.description: Cut heater power to outdoor rovers so all energy stays indoors.
choiceA.outcomeText: Outside power drain stops! Rovers sit dark and cold in the grit.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Rovers enter deep sleep modes when solar panels cannot charge batteries.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Warming only critical electronics prevents complete battery drain.
choiceA.imageCaption: The 16th American assembly flight and 112th overall American flight to the International Space Station (ISS) launched on November 23, 2002 from Kennedy's launch pad 39A aboard the Space Shuttle Orbiter Endeavor STS-113.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rovers sleeping tight! Every watt is saved for the crew.

choiceB.description: Power up the dish to get breathing tips from flight doctors.
choiceB.outcomeText: Doctors beam back great exercises! Running the transmitter uses power.
choiceB.bonusNote: Because you synced orbital relay timings on Sol 3, the dish locks straight onto the satellite using less power (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Flight surgeons on Earth monitor astronaut health 24 hours a day.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Doctors give personalized advice on nutrition, sleep, and exercise.
choiceB.imageCaption: Deep Space Station 53, or DSS-53, is a new 34-meter (111-foot) beam waveguide antenna that went online in February 2022 at NASA's Deep Space Network's ground station in Madrid.
choiceB.guideReaction: Doctor orders received! Breathing exercises help everyone relax.

choiceC.description: Turn on purple LED grow-lights so fresh salad plants sprout.
choiceC.outcomeText: Crunchy lettuce grows under purple lights! Grow-lamps draw power.
choiceC.bonusNote: Keeping your greenhouse lit back on Sol 2 protected hardy seedlings, producing instant fresh sprouts and oxygen (+5% Crew Health)!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Plants use red and blue light best, making grow-rooms glow purple.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: LED lights give plants energy without wasting heat.
choiceC.imageCaption: Situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE) instrument is about to undergo vibration testing in a lab at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California.
choiceC.guideReaction: Green sprouts! Fresh salad is growing under purple lamps.

storyNodes.guideTip: An extra 39 minutes every day adds up! Mars days are slightly longer.
storyNodes.novaHint: Fresh salad and clean air boost stamina. Balance food with batteries.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: Nuclear Core Warning
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Nuclear generators keep humming through total blackout.

consequences.text: Skipping air scrubbers on Sol 5 left itchy dust in bunks (-5% Crew Health).
Tight shelter bunks saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but cramped backs (-3% Crew Health).
Old reactor bypass overheated coils (-5% Power) and was noisy (-3% Crew Health).
Warm bunk heat on Sol 5 helped everyone recover (+4% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Just like Curiosity rolled on nuclear power, your nuclear reactor hums! You must also inspect dusty airlock suit doors.

choiceA.description: Shut down science labs and move crew to warm resting bunks.
choiceA.outcomeText: Resting helps the crew recover! Power bars hold steady.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mission managers schedule rest days when astronaut fatigue gets high.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Sleep helps human brains repair and clear mental fatigue.
choiceA.imageCaption: Engineers from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), working in a clean room facility at ISRO's U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC) in Bengaluru, India, in mid-June 2023, use a crane to align the radar instrument payload for the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) mission above the satellite's spacecraft bus so that the two components can be combined.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rest time! Cozy bunks help tired space travelers heal.

choiceB.description: Crank reactor output past normal limits to fill batteries fast.
choiceB.outcomeText: Electricity surges into batteries! Noisy pumps rattle sleeping bunks.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Nuclear cores can produce extra electricity by raising operating temps.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Running hot requires careful monitoring of sodium cooling valves.
choiceB.imageCaption: In the high bay of the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility (PHSF) at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, the multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) for NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission is attached to the MMRTG integration cart.
choiceB.guideReaction: Power surge! The batteries fill fast, but hear that loud hum.

choiceC.description: Use power to blast static grit out of airlock door seams.
choiceC.outcomeText: Clean suitports snap shut tightly! The air blasts use modest power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Suitports allow astronauts to back into suits without bringing dust inside.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Magnetic rubber gaskets seal airlock hatches against dust leaks.
choiceC.imageCaption: NASA astronauts Anne McClain (bottom) and Nichole Ayers (top), both Expedition 73 Flight Engineers, checkout spacesuit hardware in the Quest airlock and review procedures for a May 1 spacewalk.
choiceC.guideReaction: Whoosh! Clean seals keep every grain of dust outside.

storyNodes.guideTip: The nuclear reactor is our trusty engine. Treat it with care!
storyNodes.novaHint: Do not push the reactor too hard. Balance power boost with noise.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: Rover Fleet in Twilight
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Dust devils clean solar panels, but during big storms winds stay hazy.

consequences.text: Rover panel sweeps gave extra morning charge (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Orbiter communications used power (-4% Power), but Earth support lifted spirits (+5% Crew Health).
Keeping beacon mode locked preserves electricity (0% Electricity Conserved!), but dims halls (-3% Crew Health).
Shutting wing heaters saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but halls chilled crew (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Cameras show heavy dust haze everywhere! We cannot count on dust devils as winds lift water vapor skyward.

choiceA.description: Turn off rover heaters and dim hallway lights to save watts.
choiceA.outcomeText: Batteries gain a nice safety buffer! Dim halls make crew grumble.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Rovers park on high ground and sleep to save power during storms.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Parking facing the sun helps catch dawn rays when dust clears.
choiceA.imageCaption: The Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator for NASA'S Mars 2020 Perseverance rover is shown during a fit check with the rover in a payload processing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 16-17, 2020.
choiceA.guideReaction: Power saved! Dim halls, but batteries are looking healthy.

choiceB.description: Spend power heating bedrooms and scrubbing dust out of vents.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm blankets and clean air revive crew! Battery gauges dip down.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Clean, warm quarters reduce stress hormones in space crews.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Deep sleep in clean air keeps cognitive reaction times high.
choiceB.imageCaption: An illustration of MOXIE (Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment) and its components.
choiceB.guideReaction: Ahhh, warm beds and clean air! The crew feels rested.

choiceC.description: Send crew outside to wire rovers into a backup battery bank.
choiceC.outcomeText: Linked rovers feed steady power into base! Cold outdoor work tired crew.
choiceC.bonusNote: Because you pre-wired the rover power grid back on Sol 3, cables snap right in place and feed bonus charge (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: NASA designs rovers with plugs to feed power back to habitats.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Rover batteries can power emergency life support for several days.
choiceC.imageCaption: hued thermal blanketing, is seen at the Indian Space Research Organisation's compact antenna test facility in Bengaluru, India, in September 2023.
choiceC.guideReaction: Cables connected! The rovers are powering the habitat lights!

storyNodes.guideTip: Whirlwinds on Mars sometimes sweep panels clean. Not today though!
storyNodes.novaHint: Rovers have big batteries. Think about linking rover power to the base.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: Dawn Light Breaking
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Global dust storms begin clearing slowly after weeks of gloom.

consequences.text: Calling Earth gave medical breathing tips and family cheers (+6% Crew Health).
Throttling chillers saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but crew worries about fuel (-4% Crew Health).
Warmed gym gear on Sol 5 kept muscles limber for chores (+4% Crew Health).
Sleeping rovers saved standby heat (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Dim hallway lights saved battery reserve (0% Electricity Conserved!), but slowed morning focus (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: The planet-wide storm is finally thinning! Light returns after the noon blackout. Kitchen boilers and greenhouse crops need power.

choiceA.description: Turn off water boilers and eat dry ration bars to save power.
choiceA.outcomeText: Skipping cooking saves power! Dry cold bars leave crew sluggish.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Emergency ration bars provide calories without needing hot water.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Dry food bars last five years without spoiling on space missions.
choiceA.imageCaption: Documentation of the Veggie Ponds Modules while module is in Veggie Bellows.
choiceA.guideReaction: Crunchy ration bars! Saves power, but soup tastes better.

choiceB.description: Spend stored battery power to serve hot meals and warm water.
choiceB.outcomeText: Steaming soup restores crew strength! Battery meters dip lower.
choiceB.bonusNote: Extra oxygen bottles stockpiled on Sol 1 keep the busy kitchen air crisp and energizing (+5% Crew Health)!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Hot soup and warm drinks keep astronauts hydrated and cheerful.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Hydration is essential for preventing kidney stones in space.
choiceB.imageCaption: Documentation taken during removal of Germination Cap from each Veggie Ponds Module while module is in Veggie Bellows.
choiceB.guideReaction: Hot soup time! Warm bowls make everyone feel strong again.

choiceC.description: Run underground ice drills to refill drinking water tanks.
choiceC.outcomeText: Fresh melted Martian water fills tanks! The drill motors draw power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: NASA will drill into glaciers beneath red dirt for pure water.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Vast sheets of water ice lie buried just a few feet underground.
choiceC.imageCaption: At far right, Jim Smodell, a technician with SGT, shows a plant pillow from the Veggie plant growth system to Gioia Massa, NASA payload scientist for Veggie.
choiceC.guideReaction: Fresh water tanks full! That clean ice came right from Mars.

storyNodes.guideTip: Look at the horizon! The sky is turning from dark brown to peach!
storyNodes.novaHint: The storm is breaking. Decide whether to warm meals or melt water.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: First Sun on Dust
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Dust devils clean panels, but static cling keeps fine grit stuck.

consequences.text: Radio silence saved battery charge (0% Electricity Conserved!), but silence lowered spirits (-5% Crew Health).
Hearing voices from Earth on Sol 6 lifted crew focus for repairs (+5% Crew Health).
Skipping air scrubbing on Sol 5 left itchy dust circulating (-5% Crew Health).
Closing labs for medical care helped crew breathing (+4% Crew Health), using minor power (-3% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: The planet-wide storm is thinning, but no dust devils swept panels! Thick sticky red grit still coats the glass.

choiceA.description: Send astronauts onto upper catwalks to sweep dust off skylights.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sunlight pours onto greenhouse plants! The spacewalk was tiring.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts can brush solar glass with soft conductive fiber brooms.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Sweeping off dust can double the power panels generate at dawn.
choiceA.imageCaption: Red Russian kale and Dragoon lettuce are pictured growing aboard the International Space Station for the ISSGardens investigation.
choiceA.guideReaction: Sweep sweep! Bright sunlight pours into the greenhouse.

choiceB.description: Keep crew safely inside and spend power purifying water pipes.
choiceB.outcomeText: Sparkling clean water refreshes the team! Panels stay dusty for now.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: The space station recycles 98% of all water through high-tech filters.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Recycled space water is cleaner than most municipal tap water on Earth.
choiceB.imageCaption: At Space Launch Complex 576-E at Vandenberg Air Force Base in California, the Poly Picosatellite Orbital Deployer, or P-POD, assembly is imaged wrapped in its thermal insulation blanket and sheeting and the attached Anodized gold aluminum bracket interface.
choiceB.guideReaction: Pure fresh water! Staying inside keeps everyone safe and dry.

choiceC.description: Pulse mechanical vibrators on solar wings to shake off dust.
choiceC.outcomeText: Clouds of red grit slide off panels! The buzzing rattles the walls.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Engineers test ultrasonic buzzers to shake dust off solar arrays.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Rapid shaking breaks the static bond holding dry grit to glass.
choiceC.imageCaption: NASA astronaut and Expedition 74 flight engineer Anil Menon is pictured inside the Quest airlock tryng on a spacesuit to verify its comfort, mobility, and functionality.
choiceC.guideReaction: Bzzzzt! Look at all that dust slide off the solar wings!

storyNodes.guideTip: The sun is back, but the solar panels are wearing a thick dusty coat!
storyNodes.novaHint: Clean panels catch tomorrow's dawn sun. Decide how to clear dust.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: Sick Bay Alert
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Humans need clean oxygen to live, while robot rovers do not breathe.

consequences.text: Redlining reactor on Sol 6 strained valves (-5% Power) and was noisy (-3% Crew Health).
Rebooting greenhouse used power (-4% Power), but fresh greens revived crew (+5% Crew Health).
Clogged filters from Sol 4 let fine dust into sleeping bunks (-5% Crew Health).
Warming bunks and scrubbers restored crew stamina (+4% Crew Health), using power (-4% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: In 2018, Curiosity rolled safely without lungs, but our crew feels strain! Spend power on MOXIE oxygen and airlock seals.

choiceA.description: Run emergency high-speed scrubbers to clean medical room air.
choiceA.outcomeText: Emergency scrubbers clear stale air! Battery banks are sharply drained.
choiceA.bonusNote: Pure oxygen reserves built during your Sol 3 MOXIE purge supercharge sick-bay recovery (+5% Crew Health)!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Medical bays on space stations maintain positive air pressure for healing.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Clean air helps human airways heal quickly from mineral irritation.
choiceA.imageCaption: The engineering model (EM), an almost identical twin of MOXIE, is used for testing in the lab at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California.
choiceA.guideReaction: Pure clean air in sick bay! Astronauts can breathe easy.

choiceB.description: Save electricity by having tired crew wear breathing helmets inside.
choiceB.outcomeText: Power meters hold steady! Wearing heavy helmets inside tires everyone.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Sealed breathing masks protect astronauts during cabin contamination.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Filtered respirators block fine particles down to 0.3 microns.
choiceB.imageCaption: In the image, taken on June 1, 2019, an engineer in the Spacecraft Assembly Facility's High Bay 1 at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, can be seen working on the exposed belly of the Mars 2020 rover.
choiceB.guideReaction: Helmets on indoors! Saves power, but helmets are heavy.

choiceC.description: Lock down dirty lab rooms to keep bedroom air clean and calm.
choiceC.outcomeText: Sealing the lab gives lungs relief! The quiet filters use modest power.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Isolating dusty modules prevents grit from spreading through ventilation.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Closing compartment doors contains airborne dust to a single zone.
choiceC.imageCaption: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, fully suited, evaluates the mobility of his xEMU spacesuit during the Artemis Spaceflight Standard Measures Test at NASA’s Johnson Space Center on Jan.
choiceC.guideReaction: Dusty lab sealed! Bedroom air stays fresh and clean.

storyNodes.guideTip: Astronaut lungs need clean air. Breathing red dust is no fun!
storyNodes.novaHint: Crew health is critical. Clean the sick bay air or enforce masks.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: Satellites Spot Dawn
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter tracked the 2018 storm from high above.

consequences.text: Weather drone mapped flat paths, saving rover power today (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Linking rover batteries supplied extra watts (0% Electricity Conserved!), but crowded floors (-3% Crew Health).
Earlier rover panel sweeps harvest faint twilight charge (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Flushing airlock suitports cleared grit (+3% Crew Health), using power (-3% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: Cameras look murky, like on Curiosity's dusty selfie! An orbital satellite passes across the 22-minute radio delay.

choiceA.description: Pull rover batteries into base and scrape gritty outer cable plugs.
choiceA.outcomeText: Rover battery reserves boost base power! Cold airlock repairs tired crew.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Technicians use copper brushes to clear grit from electrical contacts.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Clean electrical contacts prevent voltage drops across power cords.
choiceA.imageCaption: body mobility in the xEMU spacesuit during the Artemis Spaceflight Standard Measures Test at NASA’s Johnson Space Center on Dec. (NASA/Josh Valcarcel).
choiceA.guideReaction: Plugs cleaned! Rover batteries give the habitat extra power.

choiceB.description: Send power to outdoor turbine heaters while crew eats cold rations.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warmed turbines produce steady power! Cold snacks make crew grumpy.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Heating mechanical bearings keeps lubricant fluid in subzero air.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Frozen grease can seize rotating turbine shafts completely.
choiceB.imageCaption: Deep Space Station 53, or DSS-53, is a new 34-meter (111-foot) beam waveguide antenna that went online in February 2022 at the Madrid ground station of NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN).
choiceB.guideReaction: Turbines warm! Steady power flows, but hot food would be nice.

choiceC.description: Spend dish power linking with orbiters to map thinning dust clouds.
choiceC.outcomeText: Orbital maps show sunlight returning soon! Crew morale shoots up.
choiceC.bonusNote: Your Sol 2 MRO relay calibration locks the dish on target twice as fast, saving +3% Electricity saved!
