choiceC.nasaRealDecision: High-altitude color cameras photograph dust thinning across Mars.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Tracking thinning dust tells astronauts when to resume outdoor science.
choiceC.imageCaption: Deep Space Station 56, or DSS-56, is a powerful 34-meter-wide (112-foot-wide) antenna that was added to the Deep Space Network's Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex in Spain in early 2021 after beginning construction in 2017.
choiceC.guideReaction: Good news from space! Sunlight is breaking through the clouds.

storyNodes.guideTip: The orbiter can see where the storm clouds are breaking up!
storyNodes.novaHint: Sunlight is returning soon. Check orbiter maps or warm up turbines.

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Sweeping the Solar Farm
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Opportunity had to wait for wind, but crews can sweep panels themselves.

consequences.text: Sol 4 cold fuel uses power (-5% Power), but lifts morale (+3% Crew Health).
Sol 7 cold ration bars saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but tired everyone (-5% Crew Health).
Your Sol 7 orbital scan found sunny gaps in the haze (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Clean water loops help everyone feel good (+4% Crew Health), but pumps use power (-3% Power).
Clean rover plugs help power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but suits tired the crew (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Dust is finally settling! Opportunity rover had to wait for dust devils to clean it. Your crew can put on dustproof suits and sweep panels!

choiceA.description: Two astronauts go outside with dust shields to clean Wing Array 1.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sunlight pours onto clean solar glass! Your spacewalkers return proud, sore, and dusty.
choiceA.bonusNote: Upgraded suit seals from Sol 2 block itchy red grit at the airlock, protecting crew lungs (+5% Crew Health)!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.imageCaption: NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine, left, gives a thumbs up as Amy Ross, a spacesuit engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, center, high fives Kristine Davis, a spacesuit engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, wearing a ground prototype of NASA’s new Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit (xEMU), after a demonstration of the suits enhanced mobility, Tuesday, Oct.
choiceA.guideReaction: Whoa, clean panels! More power, but sore astronauts. Great trade!

choiceB.description: Tired astronauts sleep indoors while batteries are balanced.
choiceB.outcomeText: Rest heals aching backs. The dusty panels waste some of the returning sun.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, dust in the air held in heat at night. Crews could use less heater power.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars air is very thin, and nights can drop to -90°F.
choiceB.imageCaption: The NISAR satellite, partially covered in gold-hued thermal blanketing, enters the thermal vacuum chamber at the Indian Space Research Organisation's Satellite Integration and Test Establishment (ISITE) in Bengaluru, India, on Oct.
choiceB.guideReaction: Hmm, rest feels great! Dusty panels still miss that sunshine, though.

choiceC.description: A quick shift clears frost from radiator pipes and fixes loose wires.
choiceC.outcomeText: Tighter wires waste less power. The cold dust chills the repair team.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Nuclear Power Works in the Dark
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity ran on solar power and went quiet. Curiosity kept going on nuclear power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: A nuclear core can make electricity even when the sky is dark.
choiceC.imageCaption: Avoidance camera on NASA Curiosity rover shows a fin on the radioisotope thermoelectric generator, the rear left wheel and a spring that released the dust cover.
choiceC.guideReaction: Nice fix! Less wasted power, but brrr, the crew is chilly.

storyNodes.guideTip: Solar panels need clean glass. Dust blocks the light, just like a dirty window!
storyNodes.novaHint: Sunlight is coming back. Think about what helps you use it best.

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Sunlight Returns
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Cleaning sticky dust off panels is the fastest way to get power back.

consequences.text: Sol 7 skylight sweeping gives power (+3% Electricity), but sore muscles slow everyone (-4% Crew Health).
Backup oxygen from Sol 1 keeps the air fresh during cleanup (+4% Crew Health).
Portable scrubbers use steady power (-3% Power) but protect lungs (+4% Crew Health).
Sol 7 hot meals gave energy (+4% Crew Health), but used power (-3% Power).
Your Sol 7 air purge cleared lungs (+5% Crew Health), but left batteries lower (-4% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: Sunlight is back, but sticky red dust covers your panels and greenhouse glass. Opportunity waited for wind to clean it. You can choose how to clean up or rest.

choiceA.description: Shaker frames rattle the solar farm and knock the dust off.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sheets of dust slide off the panels! The buzzing noise makes sleeping hard.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.imageCaption: NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine, left, and Amy Ross, a spacesuit engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, left, are seen with Kristine Davis, a spacesuit engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, wearing a ground prototype of NASA’s new Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit (xEMU), during a demonstration of the suit, Tuesday, Oct.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rattle, rattle! Clean panels, but the noise is tiring.

choiceB.description: Use steady power to moisten dry air and let everyone sleep.
choiceB.outcomeText: Deep sleep and moist air help the crew. Battery power drops a bit.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: NASA is testing dust shields and suit doors that keep sticky Mars dust outside.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars dust clings like static and can harm lungs indoors.
choiceB.imageCaption: NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine, left, and Amy Ross, a spacesuit engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, left, are seen with Kristine Davis, a spacesuit engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, wearing a ground prototype of NASA’s new Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit (xEMU), during a demonstration of the suit, Tuesday, Oct.
choiceB.guideReaction: Aah, sleepy time! The crew feels great, and power dips.

choiceC.description: Link the Chariot Rover and zap dust off the panels.
choiceC.outcomeText: Dust shields clear the panels with no spacewalk. Watching the power link tires everyone.
choiceC.bonusNote: Calibrated Sol 2 EDS high-voltage modules double dust-clearing speed across the arrays (+3% Electricity saved)!
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceC.imageCaption: Joshua Jones, Artemis cryogenics manager, participates in the Artemis III cryogenic propellant loading launch simulation on Wednesday, May 6, 2026, inside Firing Room 1 of the Rocco A.
choiceC.guideReaction: Zap! Power is up, and nobody had to spacewalk. Cool!

storyNodes.guideTip: Mars dust is sticky like a balloon rubbed on hair. Static makes it cling!
storyNodes.novaHint: Cleaning costs effort and rest costs power. Which matters more right now?

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Cooling Pump Trouble
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Real power machines need safety room, not nonstop top speed.

consequences.text: Pushing the core hard on Sol 6 hurt a cooling seal (-6% Power).
Shaken panels add fresh power (+3% Electricity), but the noise stressed the crew (-4% Crew Health).
Wearing helmets indoors since Sol 7 left the crew sore and thirsty (-6% Crew Health).
Heated radar gears stay ice-free (0% Electricity Conserved!), but chilly rooms stiffen joints (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Curiosity's nuclear power has no moving parts. Your reactor cooling pump just broke! Overhead, dust once over 37 miles high is finally sinking.

choiceA.description: Use stored power for oxygen, warm water, and rest.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sick-bay mist revives the crew fast. Your power reserves fall very low.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceA.imageCaption: The Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) Group of the Flight Projects Directorate at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, is responsible for designing and building the life support systems that will provide the crew of the International Space Station (ISS) a comfortable environment in which to live and work.
choiceA.guideReaction: Healing time! The crew feels much better, but power is low.

choiceB.description: Spend power and energy to launch a balloon that studies the storm.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your balloon sends great storm data to NASA. It also strains the crew and power.
choiceB.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbiters Help Mars Talk to Earth
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, NASA's Mars orbiter watched the storm grow. It also relays rover radio to Earth.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio messages take about 22 minutes to cross space.
choiceB.imageCaption: legged support structure called a quadripod onto the steel framework of the Deep Space Station 23 (DSS-23) reflector dish on Dec.
choiceB.guideReaction: Great science! Hmm, it wore everyone out. Rest helps next time.

choiceC.description: Tired engineers crawl through tunnels to join rover pumps to the reactor.
choiceC.outcomeText: The bypass steadies reactor power. The tight tunnels leave bruises and tired muscles.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceC.imageCaption: Technicians in the payload processing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida perform a fit check between NASA'S Mars 2020 Perseverance rover and its Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator on April 16-17, 2020.
choiceC.guideReaction: Clever fix! Hmm, crawling tunnels hurts. Take care of your crew.

storyNodes.guideTip: Pumps move cool liquid past the hot reactor. When a pump breaks, we need a plan!
storyNodes.novaHint: A broken part is a problem, but your crew still needs care too.

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Sky Maps and Fuel
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Sky maps from orbit help crews plan solar recovery and protect fuel.

consequences.text: Sol 7's scan found thin clouds over Ares Base (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Melted ice keeps heaters running (-4% Power) and flasks full (+5% Crew Health).
Your drone map helps field checks (0% Electricity Conserved!), but needs focus (-2% Crew Health).
Sealing the dusty lab helps breathing (+3% Crew Health), but uses power (-3% Power).

storyNodes.storyText: A relay satellite sends you clearing-sky maps. Radio takes about 22 minutes to reach Earth. Chillers that keep rocket fuel cold now compete with base repairs.

choiceA.description: Astronauts go out to tilt solar wings toward sunny spots.
choiceA.outcomeText: Tilted towers catch the returning sun right away. The dusty wind chills the crew.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.imageCaption: A crane lowers the 112-foot-wide (34-meter-wide) steel framework for the Deep Space Station 23 (DSS-23) reflector dish into position on Dec.
choiceA.guideReaction: Smart aiming! More power, but brrr, the crew is cold.

choiceB.description: Leave the towers alone and clean water and warm bunks.
choiceB.outcomeText: Fresh water and cozy bunks rebuild energy. The power gauge dips down.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceB.imageCaption: The NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite sits in a clean room facility at U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC) in Bengaluru, India, in mid-June 2023, shortly after engineers from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California and the Indian Space Research Organisation joined its two main components, the radar instrument payload and the spacecraft bus.
choiceB.guideReaction: Yum, clean water! The crew feels good, and power dips.

choiceC.description: Spend dish power on recovery plans and video letters from Earth.
choiceC.outcomeText: Seeing smiling families brightens the whole base. Smart checklists are ready too.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbiters Help Mars Talk to Earth
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, NASA's Mars orbiter watched the storm grow. It also relays rover radio to Earth.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio messages take about 22 minutes to cross space.
choiceC.imageCaption: This is an artist concept of NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter during the critical process of Mars orbit insertion.
choiceC.guideReaction: Hello, Earth! Happy faces boost the crew, and power dips.

storyNodes.guideTip: Satellites circle Mars and take pictures from above. They show where the sky is clearing!
storyNodes.novaHint: Fuel, power, and crew all need care. What will you protect first?

storyNodes.title: Sol 9: Prepare the Rocket
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: In July 2018, NASA listened daily for Opportunity as skies brightened.

consequences.text: Swept Wing 1 gives morning power (+3% Electricity), but sore workers need rest (-4% Crew Health).
Warm kitchens use steady power (-3% Power), but well-fed astronauts stay strong (+4% Crew Health).
Clean water from Sol 7 keeps everyone ready for pre-launch checks (+4% Crew Health).
Good sleep made the crew stronger (+5% Crew Health), but used some power (-4% Power).
Tilted towers catch extra morning power (+3% Electricity), but tired the crew (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: Warm golden light returns! Opportunity stayed silent in 2018, but you can power MOXIE oxygen makers. Chillers can again keep rocket fuel cold for the trip home.

choiceA.description: Use solar power to split water ice into oxygen and clean water.
choiceA.outcomeText: Fresh oxygen and clean water fill Ares Base. Your crew is ready for Sol 10!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceA.imageCaption: This diagram shows the flow of water recovery and management in the International Space Station (ISS).
choiceA.guideReaction: Deep breaths! The crew is strong, and power is lower.

choiceB.description: The crew works overtime to test the fuel chillers and power.
choiceB.outcomeText: The chillers run smoothly and power climbs. Long checklists tire the astronauts.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Mars return rockets may use liquid fuel that must stay very cold. Cooling takes steady power.

realLifeComparison.title: Your 2038 Mission vs. Real 2018 NASA Science

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: In June 2018, Opportunity lost 97% of its sunlight and could not recharge. Curiosity kept working through the storm. It has a small nuclear battery.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Future Mars bases plan to use solar panels and small nuclear reactors. Your 2038 base needed both to survive!

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: Curiosity's weather tools found a surprise. The 2018 storm made Mars days cooler. But nights got warmer, because dust trapped heat near the ground.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Mid-storm, turning down heaters worked. The floating red dust acted like a giant blanket over Mars.

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: Mars is millions of miles away. In 2018, radio messages took 6 to 22 minutes each way. A question and answer could take up to 44 minutes.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Each choice you made mattered for days. Real astronauts must handle problems on their own before Earth even knows!
